paras: The killing of Pink Hane was the fatal shooting of a Mississippi man by a quarantine guard near Lagrange, Tennessee, on the night of August 13, 1905. He was shot while trying to cross a quarantine line into Tennessee and died several hours later, and a Memphis dispatch described it as the first death from efforts to evade the quarantine in that area.

Guards had been posted along the railway near Lagrange to stop travelers from crossing the quarantine line into Tennessee. Hane was described as being 'of Mississippi', and one Texas paper called him "a negro".

According to the Memphis dispatch, a guard stationed on the line of the Southern Railway saw Hane and called on him to halt. Hane ran, and after calling twice more the guard fired. Hane died several hours later, and before his death he said he was wanted in "Joles County, Miss.", without saying why or by whom. The account of the shooting comes only from this dispatch, which named neither the guard nor any witness.
No report of an inquest, arrest or inquiry into the guard's conduct appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune carried the fullest version on August 15 under the headline "KILLED BY QUARANTINE GUARD", presenting it as a quarantine story and stating no race. The same day the Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas condensed it to one line, "A negro named Pink Hank", and reran the item the next day. A syndicated news-summary column then carried the name as Pink Hane, without race, in weeklies at Morristown, New Jersey, on August 22, Hendersonville, North Carolina, on August 24, and Abbeville, South Carolina, on September 6.
None of these papers questioned the guard's version or commented on the killing, which ran amid other quarantine and crime briefs. No Black-press coverage of the killing was found.
The victim's surname was printed as "Hane" in the Tribune and the syndicated column but as "Hank" in the Bryan Eagle, apparently a variant of the same report.

accounts.label: Memphis dispatch (guard's version as relayed)
accounts.gist: Hane tried to run the quarantine line, ignored three calls to halt and was shot by the guard; before dying he said he was wanted in Mississippi.

accounts.label: Condensed briefs
accounts.gist: A man named Pink Hank or Pink Hane was killed by a quarantine guard near Lagrange, Tenn.; the Bryan Eagle version alone identified him as 'a negro'.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headlined it 'KILLED BY QUARANTINE GUARD' and framed it as a quarantine-dodging fatality, giving the guard's calls to halt without comment and no race.
Texas, New Jersey, North Carolina and South Carolina weeklies ran it as a one-line item among miscellaneous news; only the Bryan Eagle labeled him 'a negro'.

conflicts.note: The fuller telegraph (A1) and the syndicated briefs print 'Hane'; the Bryan Eagle brief prints 'Hank', likely a typesetting variant of the same report.

info: Night of August 13, 1905 ('last night' in a dispatch dated Memphis, Aug. 14)
On the quarantine line along the Southern Railway near Lagrange, Tennessee
Pink Hane, of Mississippi (printed 'Pink Hank' in the Bryan Eagle, which called him 'a negro')
None as a cause of the shooting; he was said to be trying to 'run the line' of the quarantine. Before dying he said he was wanted in 'Joles County, Miss.', without saying why or by whom.
An unnamed quarantine guard stationed on the Southern Railway line

sources.note: Memphis Aug. 14 telegraph: Pink Hane of Mississippi shot 'last night' by a quarantine guard on the Southern Railway line near Lagrange, Tenn., after running from a call to halt; died hours later; said he was wanted in 'Joles County, Miss.' Race not stated.
quotes: Pink Hane, of Mississippi, was killed last night by a quarantine guard while attempting to run the line near Lagrange, Tenn.
The guard stationed on the line of the Southern Railway saw Hane, and called to him to halt. Hane ran, and after calling twice more the guard fired.
Before his death Hane said that he was wanted in Joles County, Miss., but did not say why or by whom.
This is the first fatality resulting from efforts to dodge the quarantine in this neighborhood.
